nearest_standard: Pullback to a rising moving average (IBD's 21-day line; Investopedia pullback)

sources.name: Investopedia: Pullback
sources.quote: A pullback is a temporary reversal in the upward price trend of a stock or other investment. It typically lasts only a few consecutive sessions and can provide an entry point for new investors when other technical indicators remain bullish.

sources.name: Investopedia: Uptrend
sources.quote: Even as the price rises, it will oscillate up and down. The moves lower are called pullbacks. If a trader or investor believes the price will continue higher after the pullback, they can buy during the pullback and profit from the ensuing price rise.

sources.name: Bulkowski, ThePatternSite: Throwbacks
sources.quote: A high volume (above the 30-day average) breakout throws back 70% of the time, on average.

summary: A short dip inside an uptrend that comes back to a rising average and holds. Investopedia says pullbacks last a few sessions and are buy spots when other signals stay bullish. The buy is the turn back up off the average; the stop sits under the pullback low. Bulkowski measures that a high-volume breakout returns to its breakout level 70 percent of the time, so a return is normal.

conventions.entry: Investopedia: buy during the pullback when the uptrend is expected to continue; limit or stop-entry orders are used.
conventions.stop: Under the pullback low (Investopedia implies a stop outside the dip; no fixed distance stated).
conventions.target: None stated; the prior high or a new swing high is the usual reference.

mistakes: Buying a 'pullback' that is really a trend change: Investopedia says a failure to make higher highs and lows means the uptrend is in doubt.
conflicts: Bulkowski uses 'pullback' for the return after a downward breakout and 'throwback' for the return after an upward breakout; the house term follows the Investopedia sense. IBD uses a 21-day line, not 20.

sources.quote: The average true range (ATR) is a technical analysis indicator introduced by market technician J. Welles Wilder Jr. in his book "New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems." It measures market volatility by decomposing the entire range of an asset price for that period.

summary: ADR% is the average of each day's high-to-low travel as a percent of price, usually over 20 days. A 5 percent ADR stock moves about 5 percent on a normal day. summary: Weinstein's four stages are basing, advancing, topping and declining. conventions.entry: Weinstein (secondary): the breakout from the Stage 1 base, ideally on volume about twice the recent average.

mistakes: Buying in Stage 1 or 3, which Weinstein calls playing against the house (secondary).

sources.name: Investor's Business Daily: How To Identify Stock Market Bottoms
sources.quote: While it's impossible to know when the stock market is going to bottom, investors can use a chart signal known as a follow-through to begin buying stocks. Here's what to look for: Following a prolonged market downtrend, look for the first up day from an index low. That's the start of a rally attempt.

sources.name: Investor's Business Daily: What Is A Follow-Through Day?
sources.quote: The start of a major stock market uptrend is difficult to identify if you are relying on headlines and news.

summary: Our text: after a low, count the rally attempt; a major index up sharply on heavier volume several days in is the green light, and it can fail. IBD matches: the first up day off the low starts the rally attempt, and the follow-through signals the start of a new uptrend. Our line 'no bottom of consequence has ever happened without one' is O'Neil's claim; the fetched IBD page does not state it.

nearest_standard: Undercut & Rally (Gil Morales / Chris Kacher, Virtue of Selfish Investing)

sources.name: Virtue of Selfish Investing (Morales & Kacher) FAQ: Moving Average Undercut & Rally
sources.quote: The mechanics of this trade are similar to a regular Undercut & Rally (U&R) move where a stock undercuts a prior low in the pattern, usually along the lows of a potential new base, and then rallies back above that low, triggering a buy signal based on the U&R.

sources.name: Bulkowski, ThePatternSite: 2B Pattern
sources.quote: The 2B bottom is a failure of price to rise far. If you wait for the second bottom to announce itself as a bottom, you'd be buying near the peak, setting yourself up for a loss.

summary: Morales and Kacher's name: a stock dips under a prior low in its pattern, usually along the lows of a new base, then rallies back above that low, and the move back above is the buy signal. Bulkowski's 2B bottom is the classical cousin: a failure of the break below to go anywhere. The shakeout clears sellers; the reclaim is the trigger.

conventions.entry: VoSI: the rally back above the undercut low.
conventions.stop: VoSI (for the moving-average version): 1 to 2 percent under the reclaimed line; for a price low, the undercut low is the selling guide.
conventions.target: None stated.

mistakes: Buying the undercut itself rather than the reclaim.
conflicts: The VoSI FAQ defines U&R inside its MAU&R answer; the dedicated 'Undercut & Rally' FAQ category is empty.

sources.quote: Breakouts on low relative volume are more prone to failure, so the price is less likely to trend in the breakout direction.

summary: Minervini's name for a base whose pullbacks get smaller from left to right (for example 20 percent, then 10, then 5) while volume dries up, until price sits tight under a pivot. sources.name: Investopedia: Wedge
sources.quote: As wedge patterns converge, the gap between the entry price and stop loss is smaller than at the start. This allows a stop loss to be placed close by, potentially yielding higher returns if the trade succeeds.

sources.name: Bulkowski, ThePatternSite: Rising Wedge
sources.quote: Price should touch (at a minor high or minor low) each trendline at least five times to outline a good pattern. That's 3 touches of one trendline and 2 of the opposite.

summary: Kell's wedge drop is the first move back below the moving averages after a strong rally, read as the end of that uptrend. The classical cousin is the rising wedge: converging up-sloping lines with volume fading, then a break below the lower line. Bulkowski uses the lowest valley in the pattern as the target after a downward break.

conventions.entry: Classical: a close below the lower wedge line.
conventions.stop: Investopedia: close, above the last high inside the wedge.
conventions.target: Bulkowski: the lowest valley in the pattern, or the pattern height subtracted from the breakout price.

mistakes: Shorting a pattern with too few touches or under three weeks (Bulkowski).
conflicts: Kell's version keys off moving averages, not wedge trendlines; the TraderLion write-up could not be fetched. StockCharts ChartSchool could not be reached from this machine (TLS handshake failure in both fetch tools).

sources.name: Investopedia: Wedge
sources.quote: A wedge pattern signals bullish or bearish reversals and has three features: converging trend lines, declining volume, and a breakout from one trend line. The two forms of the wedge pattern are a rising wedge (which signals a bearish reversal) and a falling wedge (which signals a bullish reversal).

sources.name: Bulkowski, ThePatternSite: Falling Wedge
sources.quote: The falling wedge is a poor performer as far as bullish chart patterns go. The break even failure rate is high and the average rise is low.

sources.name: Bulkowski, ThePatternSite: Falling Wedge
sources.quote: Price should touch each trendline at least five times to outline a good pattern. That's 3 touches of one trendline and 2 of the opposite.

summary: Kell's wedge pop is the first move back up through the moving averages after a stock has been stretched to the downside. The classical cousin is the falling wedge: two converging down-sloping lines, shrinking volume, then a break up through the upper line. Bulkowski rates the falling wedge a poor performer, with a high break-even failure rate and a low average rise.

conventions.entry: Classical: a close above the upper wedge line, better with heavy breakout volume (Bulkowski).
conventions.stop: Investopedia: the converging lines let a stop sit close, under the last low.
conventions.target: Bulkowski: the highest peak in the pattern, or the pattern height added to the breakout price.

mistakes: Calling a short pattern a wedge: Bulkowski wants three weeks minimum and five trendline touches.
Expecting a big run; the falling wedge's average rise is low in Bulkowski's data.
